papers.version_note: arXiv:1804.03719v3 (27 Jun 2022); title matches the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract; table of contents; Sec. 2.3 (Grover on ibmqx4, skimmed); Sec. 4 (Linear Systems: caveats paragraph and Sec. 4.4 hardware run); closing paragraphs of Sec. 12 (QAOA); Sec. 14 (Quantum SVM, whole section); Sec. 20.4 (QEC test discussion). The other algorithm sections (most of the body) were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A review that surveys 20 quantum algorithms and runs implementations of them on IBM's quantum computers, comparing simulator and hardware results.

assertions.value: In the Linear Systems section, the HHL implementation matched theoretical expectation values on the Qiskit simulator, but the run on the 5-qubit ibmqx4 hardware did not give the expected answer shown by the simulator. The authors also list overheads of HHL: loading and reading data, and the solution vector collapsing on measurement.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 4 (Linear Systems), caveats paragraph and Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 24/28)
quotes: The simulator expectation values and the theoretical values match well.
As can be seen from Fig. 16, the results from the actual run do not give the expected answer as seen in the simulator results.
This means that the HHL algorithm involves additional overheads for loading and reading data from a quantum computer [2].
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result on one 5-qubit device (ibmqx4) and one small problem; the overhead statement is the review's own summary citing another work.
assertions.reader_inference: The hardware mismatch is stated qualitatively; no numerical error is given in the passages read.

assertions.value: The review describes the quantum SVM (after Rebentrost et al. [102]) as the least-squares SVM run on quantum computers, with the kernel matrix computed by a quantum inner-product algorithm on quantum random access memory. It states that the inner product calculation for the kernel matrix cannot be done reliably in the currently available quantum processors.
quotes: The quantum version of SVM performs the LS-SVM algorithm using quantum computers [102].
It calculates the kernel matrix using the quantum algorithm for inner product [84] on quantum random access memory [60]
The inner product calculation to compute the kernel matrix cannot be done reliably in the currently available quantum processors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement by the review authors with no experiment reported in that section; the algorithm description is cited from another paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 14 has no hardware run of its own; the reliability statement is not backed by a measurement in the passages read.

assertions.value: The review states that quantum advantage for QAOA has not been achieved so far, because current devices are too noisy and the possible instances too small, and that whether QAOA can give a significant speedup or better provable approximation ratios remains open.
quotes: As of now, quantum advantage for QAOA has not been achieved yet.
Current devices are still too noisy and the possible instances too small.
Whether QAOA can achieve a significant speedup for combinatorial optimization problems, or whether it enables better provable approximation ratios, remains open.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' statement of the state of the field as of the 2022 revision; no literature search method is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is dated to the v3 revision (June 2022).

assertions.value: In the test of a simple quantum error correction scheme on IBM Q chips, the implementation did not improve the probability of interpreting the final outcome correctly. The authors state that efficient error correction must show exponential suppression of errors, which was not observed in this test.
quotes: Comparing results of the tests without and with QEC, we find that the implementation of a simple version of QEC does not improve the probability to interpret the final outcome correctly.
However, an efficient error correction must show exponential suppression of errors, which was not observed in this test.
assertions.certainty_reason: A measured result on one small IBM device and one simple scheme; the authors scope it to that test.
assertions.reader_inference: The result concerns a simple scheme on 2018-era hardware and does not bear on error correction in general.

papers.title_in_file: Emerging quantum computing algorithms for quantum chemistry
papers.version_note: arXiv:2109.02873v2 (13 Nov 2021); title matches the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract; contents; Sec. I (Introduction); Sec. II.A.1 and II.A.2 (universality, complexity); Sec. IV.C.4 and IV.C.5 (end of diagonalization methods and open problems for variational algorithms); Sec. V (opening of error mitigation). Sections on mappings, product formulas, LCU, qubitization, VQE details and the rest of error mitigation were not read.
papers.what_it_is: An advanced review of quantum algorithms for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics and eigenstates, aimed at molecular electronic structure, with their strengths and limitations.

assertions.value: The review states that circuits made only of Clifford gates give no computational advantage over classical computers through their entanglement, so advantage is to be sought in circuits that also contain T gates.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II.A.1 (Universality and limitations of digital quantum computers) (PDF p. 6)
quotes: Therefore, the entanglement that can be achieved with circuits of Cliﬀord gates alone does not give any computational advantage over classical computers.
Computational advantage is to be sought in circuits also containing T gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: The review restates the Gottesman-Knill theorem, a proved result that it cites; it is not proved in the review.
assertions.reader_inference: The review draws the consequence from the Gottesman-Knill theorem [31-33] for circuits of preparation, Clifford gates and single Pauli measurement.

assertions.value: The review states that, because a generic n-qubit unitary transformation is exactly represented with a number of single-qubit and CNOT gates it cites [27-29], quantum computers are not guaranteed to give access to a generic n-qubit state with a number of operations that scales polynomially with n.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II.A.1 (Universality and limitations of digital quantum computers) (PDF p. 6)
quotes: meaning that quantum computers are not guaranteed to give access to a generic n-qubit state with an amount of operations scaling polynomially with n.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard counting result that the review cites to other works.
assertions.reader_inference: The gate-count expression is printed as O(4n) in the text extract, with the exponent lost; the value therefore does not restate it.

assertions.value: The review states that deeper circuits with more entangling gates have significantly larger biases and statistical uncertainties from accumulated coherent and incoherent errors, and that fully addressing decoherence needs fault-tolerant computation via quantum error correction, which requires extremely low error rates and a significant overhead of physical qubits.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V (Error mitigation for near-term devices) (PDF p. 28)
quotes: Deeper quantum circuits comprising more entangling gates have signiﬁcantly larger biases and statistical uncertainties, due to the accumulation of coherent and incoherent errors,
which in turn requires extremely low error rates for qubit operations as well as a signiﬁcant overhead of physical qubits [382, 383].
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative statement by the review authors, with citations; no figures given.

assertions.value: The review states that initial estimates on a limited set of problems show quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to be resource-efficient compared to variational methods, and that an extensive numerical understanding of its performance and cost across different problems remains to be developed.
quotes: While initial estimates in a limited set of problems show QITE to be resource-eﬃcient compared to variational methods [245, 309, 321–324], an extensive numerical understanding of its performance and cost across diﬀerent problems remains to be developed.
assertions.certainty_reason: The review cites other papers for the estimates and states the gap itself; no data are shown here.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum machine learning for quantum anomaly detection
papers.version_note: arXiv:1710.07405v1 (20 Oct 2017); title matches the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract; Sec. I; Sec. II; Sec. III (pure states, including the matrix inversion and proximity measure); Sec. IV introduction and the start of IV.A. Appendices A-F and the rest of the mixed-state section were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proposes quantum algorithms (kernel PCA and one-class SVM) to detect anomalies in quantum states, with resource counts but no numerical or hardware experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum kernel PCA and one-class SVM algorithms for anomaly detection in quantum states can be performed using resources logarithmic in the dimensionality of the states, and for pure states also logarithmic in the number of training states.
quotes: We show that these two quantum algorithms can be performed using resources logarithmic in the dimensionality of quantum states.
For pure quantum states, these resources can also be logarithmic in the number of quantum states used for training the machine learning algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytical derivation of resource scaling under the stated access assumptions; no experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The task is anomaly detection on quantum data (quantum states), not on classical data such as transactions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the exponential speedups for pure states are possible as long as conditional subroutines are available to prepare the pure states and the extra requirements for quantum phase estimation and matrix inversion are satisfied.
quotes: These exponential speedups are possible as long as conditional subroutines are available to prepare the pure states and additional requirements for quantum phase estimation and matrix inversion are satisﬁed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A condition stated by the authors on their own derivation.

assertions.value: For mixed states, the authors state that a speedup in the number of training states needs further requirements, including an efficient way to generate many copies of a density matrix proportional to the kernel matrix, and that it is unclear how these can be generated with minimal assumptions.
quotes: For example, one needs an eﬃcient way of generating multiple copies of a density matrix proportional to the kernel matrix for the mixed states, which take a more complex form.
It is unclear how these can be generated with minimal assumptions.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' statement of an open problem in their own method.

papers.title_in_file: Mixed Quantum-Classical Method For Fraud Detection with Quantum Feature Selection
papers.version_note: arXiv:2208.07963v1 (16 Aug 2022), IEEE Trans. Quantum Eng. template; title matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: An applied study on a real card-payment data set that compares rule-based, XGBoost/Random Forest and QSVM fraud classifiers, proposes a quantum feature-selection procedure and a classical-quantum ensemble, all run on simulators.

assertions.value: On a balanced, heavily under-sampled subset (1500 training and 1000 test records) of 2.4 million card transactions, QSVM trained with features chosen by the authors' quantum feature selection reached test accuracy 0.78 +/- 0.01 versus 0.76 +/- 0.01 with XGBoost- or Random-Forest-chosen features, with AUC 0.81 +/- 0.01 in all three cases (Table 6, statevector simulation).
quotes: We observe that using this new feature selection by QSVM improves the outcome of the model when compared to use of QSVM with best classical features from XGBOOST and Random Forest from Table 3.
Due to data under-sampling, we have used 5 random trials to minimize bias. The average KPIs for accuracy and ACU are reported in the Table 6.
assertions.certainty_reason: One data set, simulator only, a 0.02 accuracy difference near the printed spread of 0.01, and equal AUC.
assertions.reader_inference: The Table 6 caption says 6 trials while the text says 5; AUC does not differ between feature sets. The authors' patent-pending disclosure appears on the title page.

assertions.value: With the ibm_cairo noise model and readout error mitigation enabled, the QSVM test accuracy was 0.55 +/- 0.10 and AUC 0.74 +/- 0.14 on the noisy qasm simulator, versus 0.78 +/- 0.01 and 0.81 +/- 0.01 on the statevector simulator (Table 7). The authors state the results come from a simulated quantum computer and that real hardware will be reported in a different manuscript.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV.B (Table 7) and Sec. VI (PDF p. 8/10)
quotes: We have used the noise source analyzed for the ibm_cairo backend and re-run the QSVM and enabled the readout measurement error mitigation ﬂag.
The result presented are obtained on a simulated quantum computer and the extension of this work to real hardware implementation will be collected in a different manuscript.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on a noisy simulator with a stated spread; no hardware run.
assertions.reader_inference: The noise table is the paper's only noise result and it shows a large drop; the paper's summary text does not discuss that drop.

assertions.value: On the balanced data set (10 trials each), accuracy was 77.7% for XGBoost, 80.0% for optimized XGBoost and 78.8% for QSVM-ZZ; the metaclassifier ensembles reached 79.9% (QSVM + XGBoost) and 81.0 (QSVM + optimized XGBoost) (Tables 8 and 9). Quantum and classical classifiers disagreed on 5.2% of training data and 5.5% of test data at threshold 0.5.
quotes: Classiﬁcations disagree on 5.2% of Training Data, and 5.5% of Test Data, with threshold of 0.5.
In practice, because of the size of dataset, the number of training datapoints on which the classiﬁers disagreed was limited so a simple metaclassiﬁer performed best.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulator results on one under-sampled data set; differences of one to two points.
assertions.reader_inference: The ensemble gain over optimized XGBoost alone is 1.0 point in the printed tables; the number of best features differs between models (7, 9 and 37).

assertions.value: The data are real card-payment transactions from a European cross-border portfolio (about 80% debit, 20% credit), 2.4 million in total. The authors state that because quantum hardware is limited in qubits and error rates, data dimensionality had to be reduced considerably, with a drastically reduced, under-sampled set used for the classical-versus-quantum comparison.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II (Input data set) and II.C (PDF p. 2/3)
quotes: This data set contains a total of 2.4 million payment transactions.

Moreover, when using Quantum Machine Learning (QML), Quantum Hardware is limited in number of qubits and error rates, one needs to reduce data dimensionality considerably while maximally preserving the accuracy of the model.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of the authors' own data and design choice.

papers.title_in_file: Unitary quantum perceptron as efficient universal approximator
papers.version_note: arXiv:1801.00934v2 (19 Mar 2019), including the Supplementary Material; the file name carries 2018-01 (the v1 date); title matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that defines a quantum perceptron as a qubit gate with sigmoid response, proves a universal approximation theorem for networks of such gates, and proposes an Ising-model adiabatic-passage implementation checked numerically.

assertions.value: The authors state they prove that a quantum neural network built from their sigmoid quantum perceptron is a universal approximator of continuous functions, with at least the same power as classical neural networks. In the main text the three-layer construction gives an output probability that is a linear combination of sigmoid functions of the input neurons, which by the universal approximation theorem can be used to approximate any function of them, and the supplement states the proof relies on the classical theorem and on the perceptron gate's Heisenberg-picture transformation.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Sec. II; Supplement Sec. VIII (PDF p. 1/2/7)
quotes: We prove that such a quantum neural network is a universal approximator of continuous functions, with at least the same power as classical neural networks.
by virtue of the universal approximation theorem, this implies that sout can be used to approximate any function
The proof relies on Theorem 1 and on the transformation implemented by the quantum perceptron gate in the Heisenberg picture
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem with a proof in the supplement that builds on the classical Cybenko theorem; not independently checked here.

assertions.value: The supplement states that the demonstration of universal approximation focuses on a classical limit of the approximation, neglecting the quantum fluctuations present in the correction operator. The main text states that the quantum perceptron contains the classical neural network as a limit and therefore satisfies the universal approximation theorem.
assertions.anchor: Sec. II; Supplement Sec. VIII (PDF p. 2/8)
quotes: It is important to remark that the previous demonstration focuses on ﬁnding a classical limit for the approximation, neglecting the quantum ﬂuctuations
The quantum perceptron contains the classical neural network as a limit and therefore satisﬁes the universal approximation theorem
assertions.certainty_reason: A scope statement by the authors on their own proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The result shows the quantum network is at least as expressive as the classical one; it does not show an advantage.

assertions.value: The paper states that its supplementary numerical files train classically a small quantum network to detect prime numbers, and that for the same ramp time the FAQUAD protocol is more accurate than the linear ramp (Fig. 3b, numerical).
assertions.anchor: Sec. III and Sec. VI (PDF p. 3/4)
quotes: In the Supplementary Material [36] we attach sophisticated numerical ﬁles to construct, train, and illustrate the approximation power and nesting of quantum perceptrons, training classically a small quantum network to detect prime numbers.
In Fig. 3b we observe that for the same time tf the FAQUAD protocol is more accurate;
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation results by the authors; no hardware run.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no hardware run of the perceptron gate itself; it cites earlier adiabatic-procedure demonstrations on other platforms.

papers.version_note: arXiv:1412.3646v1 (11 Dec 2014); title matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A short introductory and proposal paper that gives a quantum pattern classification algorithm for binary feature vectors based on Trugenberger's Hamming-distance subroutine, with a small simulated MNIST example.

assertions.value: The paper proposes a quantum pattern classification algorithm for binary feature vectors that follows a distance-weighted k-nearest-neighbour principle; the class is retrieved by measuring the class register, and the paper states the algorithm runs in polynomial time O(T P n), with n the feature vector size, P the number of training examples and T an accuracy threshold.
quotes: propose a quantum pattern classiﬁcation algorithm for binary feature vectors, which follows the principle of a distance weighted k-nearest neighbour method
Measuring the class-qudit then retrieves the desired class with the highest probability.
The quantum pattern classiﬁcation algorithm sketched above runs in polynomial time
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' algorithm and complexity count, without a formal proof of advantage.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper itself compares this complexity to classical kNN as a similar complexity class, not as a speedup.

assertions.value: In the authors' simulations on binarised MNIST digits, about 50% of the digits of a test set of 100 examples were classified correctly using a training set of 400 examples. The authors say the method on unpreprocessed data is only as successful as a classical majority decision on Hamming distance.
quotes: our simulations show that approximately 50% of the digits of a test set of 100 examples can be classiﬁed correctly by this method (using a training set of 400 examples)

Of course, running the algorithm on the unpreprocessed data of the binarised grey-shade pixel is only as successful as any classical algorithm executing a majority decision based on the Hamming distance between input and training vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: A small simulated example (100 test, 400 training) reported without a classical baseline number.

assertions.value: The authors state that efficient preparation of a quantum system in an arbitrary initial state is still an open problem and that questions of quantum memory devices are unresolved, and that future work would have to extend the algorithm to continuous inputs.
quotes: the eﬃcient preparation of a quantum system in an arbitrary initial state is still an open problem, and also questions of quantum memory devices have not been resolved yet.
Future works would have to extend the quantum algorithm to allow for continuous inputs
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problems stated by the authors as of 2014.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as of 2014, quantum machine learning is a premature discipline that derives its relevance from its potential to extend machine learning by a new paradigm rather than from a given theoretical foundation, and that there is as yet no fundamental theory of how quantum information can in general be exploited for intelligent forms of computing.
quotes: Despite this growing number of contributions, quantum machine learning is still a premature discipline, which derives its relevance from its potential to extend machine learning by a new paradigm, rather than from a given theoretical foundation.
there is yet no fundamental theory of how quantum information can in general be exploited for intelligent forms of computing.
assertions.certainty_reason: A 2014 authors' characterization of the field; time-sensitive.
assertions.reader_inference: Dated December 2014; do not treat as the current state of the field.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Virtual Screening in Drug Discovery: a Prospective Quantum Advantage
papers.version_note: arXiv:2204.04017v1 (8 Apr 2022); title matches the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract; Sec. I-IV in full; reference list skimmed. Appendices A-C (tables of numerical results, hyperparameters) were not read.
papers.what_it_is: An applied study that trains a support vector classifier with a quantum kernel for ligand-based virtual screening on LIT-PCBA and COVID-19 data, using simulators and two IBM processors, and defines the term Prospective Quantum Advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that they heuristically prove their quantum integrated workflow can, at least in some relevant instances, provide a tangible advantage over state-of-the-art classical algorithms on the same datasets, with strong dependence on target and feature selection method; the tests used an SVC with a quantum kernel on LIT-PCBA targets and a COVID-19 dataset.
quotes: Indeed, we heuristically prove that our quantum integrated workﬂow can, at least in some relevant instances, provide a tangible advantage compared to state-of-art classical algorithms operating on the same datasets, showing strong dependence on target and features selection method.
assertions.certainty_reason: An authors' claim (IBM Quantum co-authors) resting on simulations with a few features and selected instances.
assertions.reader_inference: The word proof is used for a heuristic argument based on empirical comparison, not a theorem.

assertions.value: In the Discussion the authors state that the proposed quantum classifiers are still classically accessible in simulations, so their approach cannot yet lead to direct quantum advantage and at best can be qualified as an interesting new quantum-inspired classical algorithm.
quotes: In doing that, the proposed quantum classiﬁers are still classically accessible in simulations, hence our approach cannot yet lead to direct quantum advantage
at best, it can be qualiﬁed as an interesting new quantuminspired classical algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: A limitation stated by the authors against their own headline claim.

assertions.value: In statevector simulation on LIT-PCBA targets and a COVID-19 dataset (AUC ROC; ten runs per setting), the authors report that QSVC tends to outperform the classical SVC and other classical methods when the number of features is 8 or higher, with QSVC up to 13% better than its classical equivalent at 16 features (Fig. 2a, ALDH1). They also report that datasets with few actives give large spread, up to ca. +/-0.3 of AUC ROC (17 actives vs 312'483 inactives for ADBR2).
assertions.anchor: Sec. III.A (Results from numerical simulations) (PDF p. 5)
quotes: Throughout this work, we observe that our QSVC method tends to outperform CSVC and the other classical methods when then number of features is 8 or higher, which also corresponds to a higher number of qubits.
Fig. 2a shows that the QSVC tends to perform signiﬁcantly better with 8+ features if compared to its classical equivalent (up to 13% better when using 16 features)
A small number of active molecules in a dataset (e.g. 17 actives vs 312’483 inactives for ADBR2) leads to large standard deviation values (up to ca. ±0.3 of AUC ROC).
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated results on selected datasets and settings with large spread on imbalanced targets; the classical baselines were run out-of-the-box.
assertions.reader_inference: The 13% figure is for the ALDH1 target with PCA features; the text does not say whether it is relative or absolute.

assertions.value: Hardware runs used 8 qubits: ADRB2 on IBM Quantum Montreal and the COVID-19 dataset on IBM Quantum Guadalupe. The Fig. 4 caption describes each as a single AUC-ROC measurement. The authors report the Montreal ADRB2 AUC ROC as comparable to the numerical simulation methods.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III.B (Results from quantum hardware) and Fig. 4 (PDF p. 7/8)
quotes: To this aim, we run simulations on IBM Quantum processors using 8 qubits for ADRB2 on IBM Quantum Montreal (Fig.3a) and for the COVID-19 dataset on IBM Quantum Guadalupe (Fig.3b).
Quantum hardware results (single AUC-ROC measurement, in brown), obtained using the IBM Quantum Montreal (ADRB2 - ANOVA, left) and Guadalupe (COVID-19 - PCA, right) quantum processors using 8 qubit

Remarkably, in our experiments we found that training and testing our QSVC algorithm on IBM Quantum Montreal provided an AUC ROC result for ADRB2 comparable to the results of all the other (quantum) numerical simulation methods
assertions.certainty_reason: One measurement per dataset on two small processors; for ADRB2 the simulation spread is large.
assertions.reader_inference: With a single measurement and a spread of up to ca. 0.3 on ADRB2, agreement with simulation says little about hardware performance.
